2025 · NAACL 2025 · Benchmarks & Evals

Benchmarking Large Language Models on Answering and Explaining Challenging Medical Questions

Two new medical-QA benchmarks — 1,524 real JAMA Clinical Challenge cases and 308 recent Medbullets Step 2/3 questions, both paired with expert-written explanations — cut accuracy below MedQA for six of seven LLMs, and a 30-example Prolific rater study finds the automatic metrics used to grade model explanations correlate only weakly with what the raters actually think of them.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

LLMs had already been reported to pass medical licensing exams — GPT-4 and Med-PaLM on USMLE-style questions — but board-exam questions and general medical-question datasets (MedQA, MedMCQA, MMLU, LiveQA-style consumer-health sets) mostly test textbook knowledge, the kind of material LLMs are well-suited to since they are trained on medical text. Real clinical decision-making is different: doctors work from atypical presentations that diverge from textbook definitions, and they want explanations, not just an answer, to understand and trust a recommendation. A handful of prior studies had already probed LLMs on genuinely hard clinical cases (e.g. physicians testing GPT-4 on JAMA-style vignettes), but at small scale, and recent large benchmarks that use real-world-aligned questions (K-QA, a benchmark of LLMs as clinical decision-makers, a rare-disease QA set) still don't ship reference explanations. Where explanations do exist, they're thin: MedMCQA's are described by the authors as low quality, ExplainCPE only covers the Chinese Pharmacist Examination, and MedExQA's explanations come from mock/online exam prep rather than real clinical cases. No existing benchmark combined real, challenging clinical cases with high-quality, expert-written explanations at any scale — which is what this paper sets out to build, twice over.

// how it works

The method

The paper constructs two English multiple-choice QA datasets, both scraped from public sources and paired with the explanations the source already contains, rather than generated or paraphrased by the authors.

JAMA Clinical Challenge (1,524 examples) comes from the JAMA Network's "Clinical Challenge" feature: real, difficult clinical cases spanning 13 medical domains, collected over a decade (July 2013 – October 2023). Each item is a long case description, a question ("What is your diagnosis?" or "What would you do next?"), four answer choices, and a discussion that explains why the correct choice is right and the others aren't. Images are excluded to keep the task text-only. Ophthalmology (378) and Dermatology (255) dominate the domain mix; Psychiatry has only 5 examples.

Medbullets (308 examples) is scraped from Medbullets Step 2/3 questions posted to X (formerly Twitter) between April 2022 and December 2023 — i.e., after MedQA's March 2021 collection cutoff, so none of these questions can appear in MedQA's training/test data. Each item has a case description, question, five answer choices, and an explanation covering each choice. The authors also build a 4-choice variant of Medbullets (dropping one random wrong option), denoted Medbullets-4, for a fair 4-way comparison against MedQA-4 — a pre-existing 4-option version of MedQA (Jin et al., 2021) that similarly drops one wrong option from the native 5-choice MedQA-5.

Seven LLMs are evaluated: two closed general-purpose models (GPT-3.5-turbo-0613, GPT-4-0613), one closed general-purpose model (PaLM 2, chat-bison-001), two open general-purpose models (Llama-2-70b-chat, Llama-3-70b-chat), and two open, medically fine-tuned models (MedAlpaca-13b, Meerkat-7b-v1.0) — MedAlpaca and Meerkat were chosen over three other candidate medical models (Meditron, HuatuoGPT 2.0, Asclepius) after a pilot showed those three trailing badly (7–25% accuracy vs. 36–49% for MedAlpaca/Meerkat on Medbullets-5/JAMA).

Three prompting strategies structure every experiment (X = case+question+choices, Y = answer, R = explanation): X→Y asks directly for an answer; X→RY is two-stage chain-of-thought (model reasons first, then is asked to commit to an answer); XY*→R gives the model the gold answer and asks it to explain why it's correct and the rest are wrong — this is the prompt used for every explanation the paper scores. X→Y is also run with 0/2/5-shot in-context exemplars under leave-one-out cross-validation.

// what they found

The results

Both new datasets are harder than MedQA under zero-shot X→Y prompting. Every model except MedAlpaca scores lower on Medbullets-4/5 than on MedQA-4/5. GPT-4 — the best model overall — drops from 78.63% (MedQA-4) to 66.23% (Medbullets-4), over 12 points; the other five non-MedAlpaca models drop between roughly 4 and 9 points at 4-choice (and up to 12.5 points at 5-choice, Meerkat). MedAlpaca is the one exception, actually improving from MedQA-4 to Medbullets-4 (45.16%→48.37%) and MedQA-5 to Medbullets-5 (39.90%→43.18%). Splitting MedQA into its Step 1 and Step 2/3 halves shows accuracy is similar across the two question types for six of the seven models, so Medbullets' extra difficulty isn't just "MedQA already mixed in easier Step 1 questions" — it's that Medbullets' more recent Step 2/3-style questions are themselves harder than MedQA's.

On JAMA Clinical Challenge (4 choices), GPT-3.5, GPT-4, PaLM 2, and Llama 3 all land close to their own Medbullets-4 numbers (within about 1–2.6 points), which the authors call a "surprising" alignment given how different real clinical vignettes are from simulated board questions. Llama 2 bucks this: it's competitive with GPT-3.5/PaLM 2/Meerkat on JAMA (44.36%) but falls well short of them on Medbullets and MedQA. MedAlpaca and Meerkat both drop sharply on JAMA relative to MedQA-4 (36.48% and 45.99%, vs. 45.16% and 64.18%), suggesting the smaller fine-tuned models struggle more with JAMA's longer, denser case descriptions.

Chain-of-thought (X→RY) is not a reliable win. It improves most models on MedQA and Medbullets, but on JAMA it only helps GPT-3.5 (48.69%→50.13%) and Meerkat (45.99%→49.86%) — the other five models (GPT-4, PaLM 2, Llama 2, Llama 3, MedAlpaca) all score the same or worse with CoT on JAMA than without it. Few-shot prompting (0/2/5-shot) fares little better: only GPT-4 and Llama 3 show a consistent benefit as shot count increases across all five datasets; GPT-3.5 and PaLM 2 barely move; Llama 2 and MedAlpaca vary or decline, and MedAlpaca can barely produce valid 5-shot output on JAMA at all given its 512-token limit.

For explanations (XY*→R prompting), the paper runs 11 automatic metrics (ROUGE-L, BERTScore, BLEURT, two BARTScore variants, three CTC metrics, three G-Eval metrics judged by GPT-4o) on Medbullets-5 and JAMA. MedAlpaca is worst on nearly every metric — except CTC Consistency, where it actually scores highest on both datasets, because its outputs are often just copied fragments of the input rather than real explanations, which inflates a metric that only checks input–output alignment. Meerkat, fine-tuned on GPT-4-generated synthetic explanations, tops CTC Relevance on both datasets. On Medbullets-5, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 lead on ROUGE-L, BERTScore, and CTC Preservation — that pattern doesn't hold on JAMA, where GPT-4 ranks 5th of 7 on all three metrics. All three G-Eval metrics rank Llama 3 and GPT-4 as the top two on both datasets. BARTScore+/++ disagree with everyone else and rank PaLM 2 first — the authors note on inspection that PaLM 2's explanations describe what each option is without precisely justifying why it's correct or incorrect, and BARTScore rewards this label-adjacent text anyway.

The paper then adds a small human-rater study: 30 randomly sampled Medbullets-5 items, explanations from GPT-4 and PaLM 2 only, 3 Prolific raters per item (Master's/Doctorate in medicine or healthcare) scoring Completeness (0–5, one point per answer choice sufficiently justified), Correctness (1–5), and Relevance (1–5). GPT-4 beats PaLM 2 on all three: Completeness 3.35 vs. 2.67, Correctness 4.45 vs. 4.35, Relevance 4.61 vs. 4.53 — consistent with most of the automatic rankings. But correlating these human scores against all 11 automatic metrics for GPT-4's explanations turns up mostly weak, sometimes negative, relationships: the best is G-Eval Coherence vs. Human Correctness at only 0.32; several metrics (ROUGE-L, CTC Consistency, G-Eval Consistency) correlate negatively with Human Completeness (-0.28 to -0.37).

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The two new datasets are a real, well-documented improvement over MedQA/MedMCQA on difficulty and recency (Medbullets postdates MedQA's collection window entirely) and on evaluability (both ship reference explanations MedQA never had). The paper also does more contamination/robustness diligence than most contemporaneous QA benchmarks: it shuffles answer-choice order for GPT-4/Llama 3/Meerkat and finds accuracy barely moves (largest change 1.95 points — Meerkat on Medbullets-5, which actually improves under shuffling, 48.70%→50.65%), and it runs TS-Guessing (masking an incorrect option and asking GPT-4/Llama 3 to guess it) to get a ≤10% success rate on both new datasets and on MedQA, arguing against verbatim memorization.

But both of those checks only cover 2–3 of the seven models, and the explanation-grading pipeline — the paper's actual novel contribution over prior QA-only benchmarks — is validated much more thinly than the accuracy numbers. The human study covers 30 items, 2 of 7 models, and only one of the two datasets (Medbullets-5; JAMA Clinical Challenge, the harder and more novel dataset, gets zero human validation of its explanations). The raters themselves are also worth flagging: they are Prolific crowdworkers screened for a Master's or Doctorate in Medicine/Healthcare and paid $12/hour (Appendix C.4) — a credential filter, with no check that they practise clinically — which matters because this small study is the paper's main evidence that GPT-4's explanations beat PaLM 2's. The G-Eval automatic metrics that carry much of the explanation-ranking story for the other five models are themselves judged by GPT-4o — a model in the same family as one of the seven models being ranked (GPT-4) — and the paper doesn't test whether that introduces any self-preference in the G-Eval scores it reports. Given that the same three G-Eval metrics are also the ones that most consistently rank GPT-4 near the top, this is a real, unaddressed confound, not just a hypothetical one.

The correlation table is arguably the paper's most important finding and its biggest caution flag at once: if the strongest positive automatic-to-human correlation is 0.32 (G-Eval Coherence vs. Human Correctness) — while the largest-magnitude entry in the table is CTC Consistency's −0.37 against Human Completeness, pointing the wrong way — and several other metrics are mildly negative too, then the automatic rankings used to compare all seven models' explanations across both full datasets rest on metrics the paper's own data says track the raters' judgment only weakly. That's a legitimate, stated limitation, but it means claims like "Llama 3 and GPT-4 produce higher quality explanations" (from G-Eval alone, with no human check on either model against JAMA) should be read as automatic-metric findings, not verified quality findings.

Finally, the excluded-images decision (noted in the paper's own Limitations) likely interacts with the domain skew in JAMA: Ophthalmology and Dermatology together are 42% of JAMA's 1,524 cases, and both specialties often diagnose from visual findings the text-only setup strips out, while Psychiatry (5 examples) is too small for any domain-level claim to carry weight. All reported accuracy numbers are single runs (no repeated seeds), so none of the differences above come with a confidence interval, though the G-Eval scores are at least averaged over 5 runs.

baselines

Seven models spanning three tiers (closed general-purpose, open general-purpose, open medical) is a reasonable spread for early 2024, but by the time this appeared at NAACL 2025 every model snapshot (gpt-4-0613, chat-bison-001 PaLM 2, Llama-2/3-70b-chat) was already superseded, and no reasoning-style model (o1, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5) is included.

contamination

TS-Guessing masked-option success is ≤10% for GPT-4/Llama 3 on both new datasets and on MedQA, and shuffled-choice accuracy barely moves for GPT-4/Llama 3/Meerkat — but both checks run on only 2–3 of the seven evaluated models, leaving GPT-3.5, PaLM 2, Llama 2, MedAlpaca untested for either.

what's missed

The G-Eval judge (GPT-4o) shares a lineage with one of the seven ranked models (GPT-4), and the human validation never touches JAMA or five of the seven models' explanations at all — so the paper's central explanation-quality claims are far less verified than its accuracy claims.

would raise confidence

Extend the human-rater study to JAMA and to all seven models, ideally with practising physicians rather than credential-screened crowdworkers; test whether a non-OpenAI G-Eval judge changes GPT-4's automatic ranking; run contamination/robustness checks on all seven models, not two or three; and evaluate at least one contemporary reasoning model.

// bottom line

JAMA Clinical Challenge and Medbullets are a genuine step up in difficulty and reference-explanation coverage over MedQA/MedMCQA, with above-average contamination/robustness diligence for a 2024-era benchmark — but the paper's most novel contribution, judging explanation quality, rests on a 30-example, 2-model, single-dataset Prolific rater study and a GPT-4o-judged automatic suite that its own correlation table shows tracks that human judgment only weakly.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. JAMA Clinical Challenge (1,524 real clinical cases, 13 domains) and Medbullets (308 post-2022 USMLE Step 2/3 questions) both cut model accuracy below MedQA for six of seven models — GPT-4 alone drops over 12 points from MedQA-4 (78.63%) to Medbullets-4 (66.23%); the sole exception differs by dataset, though: on Medbullets, MedAlpaca is the one model that improves over MedQA, while on JAMA the improver is Llama 2 instead (39.51%→44.36%), with MedAlpaca dropping 8.68 points there.
  2. Chain-of-thought prompting is not a reliable win: it helps most models on MedQA/Medbullets, but on JAMA Clinical Challenge it only improves GPT-3.5 and Meerkat among the seven models tested, leaving the other five flat or worse.
  3. The 11 automatic metrics used to grade model explanations disagree with each other (BARTScore ranks PaLM 2 first; G-Eval ranks Llama 3/GPT-4 first) and correlate only weakly with a 30-example Prolific rater study — the best correlation is 0.32 (G-Eval Coherence vs. Human Correctness), and JAMA's explanations were never checked against human judgment at all.
